en: Composed by the Śramaṇa Ji of the Great Ci’en Monastery.
Chapter Three: The Chapter on Similes (Upamā-varga).
This chapter is analyzed according to three sections: first, the statement of the purpose; second, the explanation of the title; and third, the resolution of difficulties and objections.
There are two purposes for its introduction:
first, Śāriputra, being of superior faculty, attained awakening merely upon hearing the Dharma; whereas the four others, being of middling nature, could only come to understand it through analogies.
Since the superior faculty has already been transformed by the teaching, this chapter is introduced to bring enlightenment to those of middling nature.

The *Two Treatises* state: "From this point onward, seven parables are taught for the sake of sentient beings who possess the nature of the seven kinds of afflictions, in order to counteract the seven kinds of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Furthermore, for those three types of persons who are defiled by pride yet lack [actual] afflictions—namely, those with pride regarding meditative concentration (*samādhi*), liberation (*vimukti*), and views (*dṛṣṭi*)—these are taught as the antidote, namely, the three kinds of equality."
Furthermore, it is said: "The remaining sūtras clarify the ten meanings of the unsurpassed. This means that, in general, the twenty-six chapters below clarify these three meanings.

The seven parables are contained within seven chapters: first, the Parable of the Burning House in this "Parable Chapter"; second, the Parable of the Poor Son in the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding"; third, the Parable of the Clouds and Rain in the "Chapter on the Herbs"; fourth, the Parable of the Phantom City in the "Chapter on the Phantom City"; fifth, the Parable of the Tied Jewel in the "Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples"; sixth, the Parable of Untying the Bright Pearl from the Topknot in the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices"; and seventh, the Parable of the Physician in the "Chapter on the Lifespan. Each follows its respective order and resides in its own chapter.
The three equalities consist of nine chapters: first, "Parables"; second, "Prophecy";

third, "Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples"; fourth, "Prophecy for Those in Training and Those Beyond Training"; fifth, "The Chapter on the Dharma Master"; sixth, "The Chapter on Upholding"; seventh, "The Chapter on Devadatta"; eighth, "Never Disparaging"; and ninth, "Seeing the Jeweled Stupa."

The first eight chapters all contain predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) and explain the equality of the initial vehicle; subsequently, within the "Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa" chapter, the two kinds of equality regarding the phenomena of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, as well as the body, are explained together.
These Ten Supreme [Teachings] consist of twenty-one chapters. The first nine Supreme [Teachings] comprise seven chapters: first, the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs";
second, the "City of Illusion," which contains the second and third Supreme [Teachings];

third, the "Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples"; fourth, the "Vision of the Jeweled Stupa"; fifth, the "Peaceful Conduct"; sixth, the "Emergence from the Earth"; and seventh, the "Life Span," which contains the eighth and ninth Supreme [Teachings].

Among the seven preceding chapters, excluding the second and the seventh, each of the remaining five chapters constitutes one instance of the "unsurpassed" (anuttara). The remaining sūtras constitute the tenth unsurpassed; that is to say, the other fourteen chapters are all the tenth unsurpassed.
Within this, there are two powers:
first, the power of the Dharma; second, the power of cultivation.
The power of the Dharma has three grades:
First, "Discriminating Merit"; second, "Merit of Rejoicing"; third, "Merit of the Dharma Master.
Within the power of practice, there are further seven powers, totaling eleven chapters:
first, the power of upholding has three chapters—first, "The Dharma Master"; second, "Peaceful Practice"; and third, "Exhortation to Uphold."
Second, the power of teaching consists of one chapter, namely the "Power of Supernatural Abilities" (Śakti-parivarta).
Third, the power of practicing asceticism consists of one chapter, namely the "Medicine King" (Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta).
Fourth, the power of practicing asceticism for the sake of transforming sentient beings consists of one chapter, namely the "Wonderful Sound" (Gandavyūha-parivarta).
The fifth, the power of protecting sentient beings from various perils, consists of two chapters:
first, "Universal Gateway of Avalokiteśvara," and second, "Dhāraṇī.
The sixth, the power of superior merit, consists of one chapter, namely, "The Past Deeds of King Wonderful Adornment."
The section on the Power of Protection (*rakṣā-bala*) consists of two chapters:
first, the "Samantabhadra" chapter, and second, the "Entrustment" (*parindanā*) chapter.

The subsequent ten "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) items correspond to the initial seven metaphors; the remaining three "Equalities" (*samatā*) are termed the "residue of the unsurpassed. Therefore, after explaining the seven metaphors and the three equalities within this treatise, it states: "The remaining sūtras clarify the meaning of the unsurpassed."

The tenth "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) is the remainder of the preceding nine kinds of unsurpassed; it is termed the "lower remainder. Therefore, the root treatise explains the tenth unsurpassed as follows: "The tenth is the supreme and wondrous power; it is taught in the *Sūtra* as the remaining portion of the unsurpassed."
The term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) has two meanings:
first, a remainder of the text, because it has not yet been explained;

second, a remainder of the meaning, because although the meaning was previously explained, it is still not exhaustive, as there remains another aspect to be considered; thus, explaining it again is termed a "remainder of the meaning."
For fear of excessive prolixity, these matters are omitted here and will be explained in detail one by one in the subsequent chapters.

This applies to the seven chapters—the "Herbs," "The City of Illusion," "The Five Hundred Disciples," "The Jeweled Stupa," "Encouragement of Devotion," "Peaceful Practices," and "Life Span"—because their texts or meanings are reiterated therein.

Regarding these seven similes: ordinary beings and those still in training (śaikṣa) are said to possess afflictions; they have seven kinds of superior conceit (adhimāna) rooted in defilement. To counteract this, seven parables are taught. For instance, taking a conjured city (nirmāṇa-pura) for a real city is like regarding the worldly meditative attainments (samāpatti) sought after as true liberation (nirvāṇa), because one clings to the perfection of those who are no longer in training (aśaikṣa) and thus has nothing further to seek.

Those of the two vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning are called "persons free from afflictions. Yet they possess three kinds of defiled pride based on the clinging to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*). While such clinging to dharmas—such as regarding their samādhis, liberations, and views—is not termed "defiled" in relation to the two vehicles, once these individuals have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] and become bodhisattvas, this clinging to dharmas is termed "defiled" for them; thus, they are said to possess "defiled pride that is nonetheless free from afflictions."
The commentary translates "perversion" (*viparyāsa*) with this intended meaning.
As for the sense of "unsurpassed," it may be said to exist within the Mahāyāna, but it does not exist in the other vehicles.
Because of these three vehicles, distinctions are taught, as there are differences in their doctrine, reasoning, practice, and fruition.

The treatise cites the Buddha’s words that "not departing from my body" constitutes the unsurpassed meaning; therefore, this meaning is not taught within the two vehicles, as they are incapable of understanding it.
By virtue of this unsurpassed [vehicle], it constitutes the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna); these should be assigned to the respective chapters as appropriate.

Regarding the seven types of sentient beings fully possessed of afflictions: first, those who seek power give rise to the first kind of perversion—the pride of overestimating their attainment of merit—and they seek the sublime realms and karmic rewards of gods and humans while worldly afflictions burn intensely; for them, the Parable of the Burning House is taught.

Wealth, nobility, and sovereign mastery are called "power. This refers to ordinary worldlings who seek the sublime external fruits of gods and humans as well as internal retributive results, yet remain unaware that their afflictions are fiercely burning and cooking them. For this reason, the parable of the burning house is taught; for the power of gods and humans is scorched by afflictions just as a house is consumed by fire.

The World-Honored One now speaks of two chariots; these are the worldly roots of goodness and samādhi, which provide a provisional understanding of bodhi to enable one to exit the house, and subsequently lead one gradually into the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha. Therefore, the Treatise says: "As for the first person, by means of the various worldly roots of goodness, samādhis, and merits, he is skillfully made to play, and later led into nirvāṇa."

In this context, it is not said that the true wisdom of the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—which is the direct realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) within the path of liberation—is called "worldly samādhi" or a "provisional understanding. This [realization] is like a goat or a deer, not the body of the chariot itself. Because the mind is coarse when subsequently entering a worldly meditative concentration (*laukika-samādhi*) after that [path], one does not see the true wisdom or the suchness (*tathatā*) of the emptiness of persons; rather, one sees only that afflictions, karma, and future suffering do not arise, and the mind consequently transforms into the conceptual understanding of *nirvāṇa*.

The cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) attained within the fundamental contemplation realized by right wisdom is metaphorically termed a "transformed city" (*nirmita-pura*); it is not said that this city is a transformation produced by provisional contemplation, because such a city does not bring an end to suffering.

Now, it is explained that at the stage of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), the transformation of conceptual understanding is termed "worldly roots of goodness" (*laukika-kuśala-mūla*) and samādhi. Through various merits such as pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and joy (*prīti-sukha*), one metaphorically plays with the sheep and deer carts and the metaphorical "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*). Subsequently, by transforming [the teaching] into the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), one causes them to enter the Great Nirvana of the Buddha; upon reaching the state of Buddhahood, being able to enter the ox-cart is precisely these two wisdoms, which is itself Bodhi, and the Nirvana entered is the Precious Place (*ratnasthāna*). As for the later parable of the illusory city (*nirmita-nagara*), because those of the Two Vehicles cling to it, their delusions and sufferings do not arise, and thus it is called Nirvana. In reality, however, Nirvana is the realization of correct wisdom within the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); therefore, it is said that when the caravan enters the illusory city, the merchants are all exhausted and find rest.

Because the various wisdoms of the past and future are all unable to comprehend all phenomena, they are in reality not the "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvajñatā*); it is merely that the names of the sheep and deer carts are spoken of, yet one does not see them actually ascending. This is because these worldly samādhis and roots of goodness are taught for the purpose of allowing beings to play within them.

The followers of the Two Vehicles grasp this as being two chariots, yet it is not actually the substance of a chariot; just as the four inversions arise for those of the Two Vehicles, which are seen to be otherwise through correct contemplation and only later understood as such, so too is the case with the attachment arising from these conditions regarding the "transformed city."
Now, to counteract the pride of those who seek power and wrongly seek merit, this parable of the chariot is taught; thus this chapter follows.
The remaining meanings will each be explained in their respective chapters.
Regarding the explanation of the names [of the chapters]: "Pì" (譬) means comparison or analogy; the *Yùpiān* states, "To compare categories in order to bring about mutual understanding.
"Yù" (喻) means to open up or to enlighten; the *Yùpiān* states, "It means to enlighten and to admonish."

Now, by taking the immediate traces of the mundane world as examples to illustrate the profound principles of the supramundane, I shall open up what has not yet been spoken and enlighten those who are previously deluded. Because these explanatory illustrations are called "parables," this chapter is named the Parable Chapter (*Avadāna-parivarta*); alternatively, because the illustration itself is the parable, it is named the Parable Chapter.
To resolve the objection: First, a question is asked:

"Since this uses a metaphor to clarify the principle, it should be named the 'Parable Chapter' (Paryāya-parivarta); previously, since the Dharma was directly manifested, it should have been named the 'Dharma Chapter'.
Answer:

While it is logically true that preceding and succeeding cases should follow one another, why labor over the differences in their establishment? "Skillful means" (*upāya*) is a specific term within the Dharma, whereas "analogy" (*aupamya*) is a general designation for comparison; since the general and the specific differ, their respective names are distinct, and thus they cannot be treated as equivalent.
Second question:
Why are these seven similes uniquely designated by this name alone, while the others are accompanied by additional titles?
Answer:

Although there are seven types of parables, because this is the first, its general designation serves as its own specific name; for in other chapters, they are not designated simply as "parable" (*aupamya*).
Three questions arise:

Since the middle-capacity [disciples] receive [the teaching] through the *vyākaraṇa* (prediction) that marks their faith and understanding, and the superior-capacity [disciples] receive it through the prediction that logically requires a separate opening, why does the beginning of this chapter rely upon the events of Śāriputra’s reception and prediction?

In the response, because the faculties of the middle-capacity [disciples], their comprehension (*prativedha*), and the recorded teachings (*udgraha*) are extensive in text and long in meaning, they are treated separately; since Śāriputra was not so, this is stated by way of him as a representative.

Furthermore, it is because the parables were presented only after Śāriputra’s comprehension and the request for instruction that this initial section is used to clarify his comprehension and the recording of the teaching.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “At that time, Śāriputra” up to “attained what he had never before experienced,” the commentary states:
Within this chapter, the main text is divided into two sections.

Initially, Śāriputra hears the Dharma, experiences joy, articulates his realization, and receives a prediction; subsequently, the Buddha extensively employs parables to transform those of middle capacity.
The initial passage belongs to the first cycle, the teaching of the One Vehicle through direct discourse (*dharmadeśanā*).

The first cycle consists of four parts. Having concluded the aforementioned Dharma-exposition, the second section below concerns Śāriputra’s reception and understanding of the Dharma, his self-reproach, and the arising of joy; this contains two sub-sections:
first, the prose, and second, the verses.
The prose section has two parts:
first, the indication that joy arises from hearing the Dharma; second, the explanation of the reason for this joy.
This is the first part.

According to the common worldly interpretation, "yong" (踊) means to leap up, and "yue" (躍) means to bound; to leap with raised feet is the height of joy. One leaps for joy because one hears the True Way and gives rise to skillful means;

one rejoices because one praises what the heart desires; one rises immediately because one manifests the Great Mind; one joins the palms because the mind accords with what has been taught; and one addresses the Buddha because, with single-minded intent, one seeks instruction, gazes upon the Honored Countenance, and sets forth what was harbored in the heart.
"The Sound of the Dharma" refers to the verbal teachings of the Mahāyāna.
Having never heard it before, one attains what is unprecedented.
Furthermore, there are three reasons for rejoicing:
First, upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, their minds became as tranquil as the ocean; they knew that the Buddha was not a Māra, and thus they rejoiced.
Second, upon hearing that the present single reality explains the past three provisional means—that the three are the cause for the one—they rejoiced.
Third, upon hearing the Buddha say that all twelve hundred arhats shall also become Buddhas, they rejoiced.
Regarding the passage from "For what reason? up to "immeasurable knowledge and vision," the commentary states:
The following explains the reasons for his joy, which are fourfold:

First, lamenting over having lost the Great Dharma; second, rejoicing at occupying a minor stage; third, delighting that one has now heard it and thus afflictions are exhausted; fourth, knowing oneself to be a child of the Buddha and that the Way is accomplished.
This is the first [character].
"Yu" (豫) means to enter or a pass. According to the *Yupian*:
"Yu means to prepare beforehand; it signifies preparation and early action."
The *Qieyun* states: "If [the character] is written as 逸, it should be 豫; it ought correctly to be 預.
The *Erya* defines it as: "預 means to reach, to arrive at, or to join with."
The ancient text reads "yu" (with); the *Zuozhuan* says, "The Duke must be with us.
"Gan" (to stir) means to incite.
"Shang" (to grieve) means to sigh.

In the past, we heard of the matter of Bodhisattvas receiving such predictions, yet we did not enter into them; in the past, we heard of the category of those receiving predictions, yet we did not reach the actual matter of the prediction. For this reason, our feelings of agitation and resentment are profound; we grieve and lament that we have lost the Tathāgata’s five kinds of knowledge and vision, or perhaps lost the knowledge and vision of the Tathāgata’s nature of wisdom and its characteristics.
Regarding the Sūtra passage: "World-Honored One, I have always dwelt alone... until I was seen and delivered," the commentary states:
This is an expression of praise arising from dwelling in a lower stage; it consists of two parts.
The first part praises abiding in the Lesser Vehicle, while the latter part reproaches oneself;
this is the former.
"Constantly" (chang) means eternally.
"Every" (*mai*) refers to frequency or repetition; it is not a term denoting a fixed number.
"Entering" (*ru*) means realization.
"Dharmatā" refers to the suchness (*tathatā*) of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), for they realize it together.
Since both I and the bodhisattvas are equally able to realize and enter the suchness of selflessness, why does the Tathāgata alone deliver us through the Lesser Vehicle?
Or, "nature" may refer to essence; that is, we are alike in entering the category of the essence of the Buddha-dharma.
In some versions, the character "cháng" (tasted/attempted) is used, meaning "formerly experienced.
The sutra states: "This is our own fault, not that of the World-Honored One.
The commentary says:
There are three parts to the subsequent self-reproach:
first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion.
This is the heading.

"Fault" (jiù) refers to transgression or error; it denotes my own offenses. The pronunciation of "jiù" is reversed from "jù" (巨久反). The character is composed of "person" (人) and "each" (各); when individuals act in opposition to one another, faults and errors are thereby produced.
Regarding the passage from "Why is this so? to "and thereby attain deliverance," the commentary states:
This explains the underlying cause.
The "causes" refer to the causal practices for achieving great bodhi; that is to say, the four bodhisattva practices within the seventh stage:

first, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa); second, the perfections (pāramitā); third, the various supernormal powers (abhijñā); and fourth, the maturation of sentient beings (sattvaparipācana).

Therefore, Kāśyapa said: "One does not take pleasure in the Bodhisattva-dharmas, the playful exercise of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), the purification of Buddha-fields, or the maturation of sentient beings. Thus, the causes for perfect enlightenment are precisely these four practices.
"Waiting" (*pratīkṣā*) carries the meaning of looking forward to, yearning for, and desiring.

Śāriputra said of himself: "If we had looked forward to, desired, and yearned for the cause of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, the Buddha would certainly have delivered us by means of the Mahāyāna; however, because we did not give rise to such longing or expectation regarding that great cause, the World-Honored One did not deliver us by means of the Mahāyāna."
Furthermore, the bodhicitta is briefly categorized into three types:
first, revulsion toward the conditioned; second, the seeking of enlightenment; and third, profound mindfulness of sentient beings. One should thus abide, thus practice, and thus subdue the mind.
The Sūtra says: "However, we have reached the point of reflecting upon attaining realization.
The Commentary states:
This constitutes self-reproach.

However, because we did not understand that the Buddha’s teachings were spoken according to his skillful means and as suited to the occasion, we believed and practiced them immediately upon first hearing them, and sought realization through contemplation; thus, the Buddha did not deliver us by means of the Mahāyāna, and this is our own fault.
The Sūtra says: “World-Honored One, you have most excellently attained peace and security.
The commentary states:
Rejoicing now at having heard [the teaching], all afflictions are exhausted.

"Kai" (克) means "exclusive devotion. Since ancient times, those who practiced the Lesser Vehicle were exclusively devoted to self-reproach and did not seek the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, they doubted that Bodhi was not their lot and failed to give rise to joyful aspiration;

or else, believing that they themselves had already attained liberation and were no different from the Buddha, they heard the Buddha now say that the Dharma attained by the Buddha is profound and difficult to understand, and that the Two Vehicles do not comprehend it, thereby suspecting the Buddha was a Māra. Now, having heard the teaching of one reality and three provisional means, they know that their former practice of the Lesser Vehicle served as the cause for the Great Vehicle. Thus, their remorse is severed; knowing that they shall become Buddhas and possess a share in Bodhi, and realizing that the liberation they previously attained was merely a skillful means of the Buddha, their doubts are likewise severed. Their minds open and their intentions are resolved; body and mind are at ease.

"Serene" (*tai-ran*) refers to the appearance of being peaceful, stable, and joyful; because one is free from doubt and regret, one is swift and at ease. If doubt and regret were to arise, one would always be unsettled; how, then, could one be serene?
"Cutting off" (duàn): the first character is read as túguǎn, meaning to sever or to terminate; it is also read as dōuluàn, but here we follow the former.
Question:

Doubt arises from conceptual discrimination and is eliminated upon entering the path of vision (darśana-mārga); remorse is accompanied by much sorrow and is abandoned upon the departure from desire (vairāgya).
"How is it that for Śāriputra, these two have now been eliminated?
Answer:
"The doubt regarding the afflictions is exhausted upon becoming a stream-enterer."
Afflictions accompanied by remorse are eliminated once one is free from desire.

Now, regarding those types of mental states associated with the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), doubt arises as a result of karmic maturation (*vipākaja*); this is like the case of Arhats who doubted whether it was black salt or not.
As for doubt concerning specific matters, the term "evil doing" (*kaukṛtya*) is appropriately named "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*); there is no error in this reasoning.

The essence of this *kaukṛtya* (remorse) is precisely wholesome *hrī* (moral shame), because it involves a light rejection of violence and evil; or it is precisely *nirveda-prajñā* (wisdom of aversion), as both are a portion of non-attachment (*alobha*), and it also consists of the examination of the mind and mental factors.

However, the nature of remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is necessarily coarse and agitated; therefore, it is abandoned upon the transcendence of desire. When remorse exists in one who has transcended desire, it must be *akusala* (unwholesome). The name "remorse" is applied here based on its fruit; for how could one who has already transcended desire not feel aversion toward it?
The Sūtra says: "Only today do I know that I have attained a portion of the Buddha-dharma.
The commentary states:
This means that one knows the Son of the Buddha has accomplished the Way.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 84, contains six phrases, which state: "He is a great lion; born from the Buddha’s womb, born from the Buddha’s mouth, born from the Buddha-dharma, transformed by the Buddha-dharma, and having attained an equal share of the Dharma."
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states, "One obtains the surplus wealth of the Buddha," which consists of four phrases.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains: "The first is the general phrase; the subsequent five are the specific phrases."

The phrase "born from the womb" excludes ordinary beings who are inferior sons; it refers to those truly born from the womb of the Buddha through the attainment of noble wisdom. This is not like ordinary beings, who are merely fostered sons of the Buddha, for all sentient beings are children of the Buddha. Since the Buddha does not personally procreate them and they are not born from his physical womb, being born from the Dharma of the Buddha is what constitutes true birth.

Furthermore, those of the two vehicles and others do not produce children from their wives as a maidservant produces a child; therefore, the subsequent sutra says, "If they were like my own children. Bodhisattvas of the first stage (prathamabhūmi) are born into the family of the Tathāgata because they realize the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); thus, they are children born of a wife. Prior to this, they are not children born of a wife and are therefore called "not womb-born" (an-udaraja).
Now, having resolved upon the Great Mind, one shall be born from within the Dharma-realm of the Bodhisattvas; this is collectively termed "birth from the womb.

Those "born from the Buddha’s mouth" are so called because they are born from the sound of the preaching of the Dharma; their essence is the wisdom derived from hearing, for they are produced by relying upon the teachings.

That which is produced from the Buddha-dharma arises from appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) and practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*); its essence is comprised of the two types of wisdom—wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*)—since it arises accordingly by taking either principle (*nyāya*) or teaching (*deśanā*) as its object.
Those who are transformed by the Buddha-dharma attain the semblance of the Dharma through the path of the Dharmakāya.
The path of the Dharmakāya refers to the two causes—the merit and wisdom—of all Bodhisattvas; I am likewise so, for I am established from within those two causes.
The Dharma-body has two aspects,
because the meanings of the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna differ.
Those who have attained the equal portion of the Dharma are so called because they resemble the Dharma in that they enjoy the wealth and treasures of untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma).
"Dharma" refers to the Jewel of Dharma, or the seven noble riches—namely, faith, ethical discipline, learning, renunciation, wisdom, shame, and dread of blame—and so forth.

"Portion" (bhāga) means a remaining portion or a categorized division. Since the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to utilize these riches of Dharma, and I am likewise similar to them, having obtained a portion of the remainder of the untainted Jewel of Dharma for my own enjoyment, I am, according to my respective capacity within the stages of the Two Vehicles, already taught as one layer above ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and am truly a child of the Buddha.

Now, acting as a bodhisattva, one looks toward the stages of the two vehicles and further teaches them in a single layer; those who are true sons of the Buddha and others may explain this according to the principle.

He further explains: "These various phrases demonstrate the perfection of superior birth (*abhyudaya*) and the perfection of birth resembling the father's dharma. Among the latter five phrases, the first three demonstrate the perfection of superior birth, while the final two demonstrate the perfection of birth resembling the father's dharma."
"Higher rebirth" (*abhyudaya*) refers to a superior physical existence; it is "similar to the father" because one inherits the father's body and utilizes the father's wealth, being thus alike to him.

Within this higher rebirth, the first phrase excludes defects of the vessel: [the Buddha] is born from the womb of the Buddha’s perfect wisdom, thereby excluding birth from the foul vessel of the womb as found among worldly beings.
The second phrase excludes [the Buddha] from being born from the impurities of semen and blood; he is born from the mouth of the Buddha, for his self-nature is not constituted by semen and blood.

The third phrase excludes the notion that his arising is due to lustful craving rather than the True Dharma; ordinary beings exist through the nourishment and moisture of lustful craving and thus arise from what is not the True Dharma, whereas he now arises from the True Dharma, not from lustful craving or that which is not the True Dharma.

The fourth phrase reveals the dharmas that are similar to its own essence; it is established by way of the path of the *dharmakāya* and inherits the excellence of the *dharmakāya*'s own essence, just as one establishes nobility by inheriting the lineage of a Brahmin.

The fifth phrase concerns the enjoyment of similar dharmas; that is, enjoying the dharma-wealth of the untainted Buddha, just as in the world one enjoys the resources and utensils provided by one's parents.

Within this, there are four [phrases], with the second being absent. The combined transformation and birth are taken together as a single phrase. Previously abiding in the provisional stage, one was not a true son of the Buddha; now, seeking the position of reality, one is finally "born from the womb. This is the great purport of the text of this sutra.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "It is not like the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who are like ignorant maidservants.

Furthermore, there is another interpretation which claims that the preceding four sections correspond respectively to the four meanings of "receiving," "revealing," "awakening," and "entering" mentioned earlier; however, upon careful examination of the nature of the Dharma, this principle is not necessarily so.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, “At that time, Śāriputra... until all nets of doubt were completely removed,” the commentary states:
These twenty-five and a half verses are divided into two parts.
The first two and a half verses constitute the introduction, while twenty-three verses constitute the explanation.
The introductory section has two parts:

the first verse praises the attainment of a state of unprecedented joy and the removal of doubt; the subsequent one and a half verses explain the attainment of the unprecedented and demonstrate the exhaustion of sorrow and regret.
This is the first [point].
Previously, he doubted that he had no share in Buddhahood; now, having heard that he can attain it, his doubt is removed.
Because doubt hinders sentient beings and makes liberation difficult, it is likened to a net.
The Sūtra says: "From of old I have received the Buddha’s teaching; even upon hearing it now, my grief and affliction are likewise removed.
The commentary states:
This explains that what has never before been attained has now been realized, manifesting the exhaustion of sorrow and regret.
It means that since the past, I have been under the Buddha’s teaching, thinking that by abiding in the Lesser Vehicle I would never attain the Great; therefore, I felt sorrow and regret.
Having heard this sutra preached, I now know that I have not lost the Mahāyāna, for because of the causes of the Mahāyāna I had previously cultivated, my regrets are now exhausted.

The Buddha’s voice possesses rare and wondrous efficacy, capable of removing the distress of sentient beings' afflictive obscurations; although I have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), hearing it now likewise enables me to subdue and eliminate the distress of clinging to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).

In this context, "sorrow" refers to the sorrow of not becoming a Buddha; one interpretation holds that it is the sorrow of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Because one does not abandon desire for it—just as Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja did not abandon his habit of harsh speech due to his failure to relinquish attachment to phenomena—the same applies accordingly to the preceding doubts and regrets.

Second, as for the claim that it is actually *daurmanasya* (sorrow), this refers to the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) associated with *kaukṛtya* (remorse) that is characterized by aversion and disdain; it is designated by the name "sorrow. Alternatively, it may refer to the neutral (*avyākṛta*) or wholesome (*kuśala*) sorrow belonging to the category of clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), which is not abandoned upon the attainment of detachment (*vairāgya*). The affliction (*upāyāsa*) associated with sorrow is itself the remorse of sorrow; it is not a primary affliction (*kleśa*).

Regarding the sūtra passage, “I was originally attached to false views, yet I have attained realization through the dharma of emptiness,” the commentary states:
The following four verses eliminate remorse; these are divided into two parts.

The first one and a half verses describe how he formerly abandoned the heterodox to return to the orthodox; the latter two and a half verses describe how he now recognizes the Small Vehicle to turn toward the Great Vehicle.
This is the first part.

In his former life, the non-Buddhist Śaṃjaya led one hundred disciples. Later, he returned to the Buddha, left the household life, and realized the principle of the emptiness of persons, attaining the title of Arhat and becoming known as a teacher of Brahmins. This is called "extracting the heterodox and attaining the realization of the Dharma of Emptiness."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra, “At that time, the mind said to itself: ‘This is not yet true parinirvāṇa’,” the commentary states:
The following two and a half verses describe how [the Bodhisattva] currently recognizes his own limited capacity and turns toward the Great Vehicle; this section is divided into two parts.
The first verse refers to the limited knowledge of the Lesser Vehicle, while the latter half refers to the realization of the Great Truth.
This is the former.
It is because in the past, one did not recognize that what was called "true extinction" was merely conventional.
The Sūtra says: "When I attain Buddhahood... until it is forever extinguished without remainder.
The Commentary states:
One knows that the Great [Vehicle] constitutes true extinction.

When one attains Buddhahood, one is inwardly endowed with all the primary and secondary marks and outwardly becomes an object of refuge and veneration for sentient beings; only then does one achieve the eternal exhaustion of the two kinds of birth-and-death such that no further outflows remain. Therefore, it is known that the Mahāyāna constitutes true cessation (*nirvāṇa*).
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, “The Buddha, amidst the great assembly... all doubts and regrets have been entirely removed,” the commentary states:
The following seven and a half verses praise the present cessation of doubt, which is divided into two parts:

The first verse concludes the preceding section on the exhaustion of remorse and explains the basis for the subsequent removal of doubt; the following six and a half verses correctly explain the removal of that doubt.
This is the first [of those].
The Sūtra says: "From first hearing what the Buddha has taught... up to 'is this not to disturb my mind?'"
The commentary states:
The following six and a half verses correctly explain the removal of doubts. This section further divides into two parts:
the first verse describes the origin from which the doubt arises, and the subsequent five and a half verses correctly explain the extinction of that doubt.
This is the first [point]. Previously, the Buddha taught the three vehicles (*triyāna*), which I have already attained;

now he teaches them as one, which contradicts what was originally taught. He says that what I have attained is not the true fruit of cessation (*nirodha*). Therefore, my mind is startled, and I think: "The Buddha is a Māra who is confusing and disturbing my mind. This doubt concerns the facts (the phenomena) and is termed "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*); because it does not concern the underlying principle (*tattva*), it is not an affliction (*kleśa*).
Alternatively, it may be that former anxieties and doubts were all manifested as arising; it is not that Śāriputra still possessed anxiety and doubt.
As the Sūtra says: "The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, [taught] until my web of doubts regarding what I have heard was severed."
The commentary states:
The following five and a half verses resolve doubts and eliminate [them]. Among these, there are four parts;
the first verse demonstrates that the Buddha’s speech is skillful and the mind is at ease, whereby doubt is severed.
Two verses clarify that the Buddhas of the three periods of time equally teach skillful means, thereby severing doubt;
one verse explains that the Buddhas' teachings are identical, thereby severing doubt;
and one and a half verses show that the path of the Buddha differs from the tracks of Māra, thereby severing doubt.
This is the first [section].
The Buddha’s teaching is twofold:
first, the literal exposition (dharmadeśanā), and second, the illustrative exposition through parables (aupamyadeśanā).
"Various conditions" refers to explaining the principle through the Dharma; "various analogies" refers to explaining by means of comparison.
While externally manifesting these two skillful modes of teaching the Dharma, his inner mind remains as firm and unmoving as the ocean; thus, his doubts are severed.

If one's speech is unskillful, if the principles and metaphors deviate from the core tenets, if the mind is wavering, or if wisdom is deluded regarding the true realm, then internal and external obstacles may arise and doubt will be difficult to extinguish;
now, however, it is not so, and for this reason, doubt is severed.
Regarding the sutra passage from "The Buddha spoke of the past" up to "expounding such a Dharma," the commentary states:
This clarifies that the Buddhas of the three periods of time all equally teach the skillful means (upāya), and thereby doubt is severed.

The first verse concerns the past, while the subsequent verses concern the two periods of the future and the present; the former are all provisional means (*upāya*), while the latter constitute the ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*). This thus summarizes the preceding chapter’s teaching on the identity of the Buddhas across the three periods of time.
The assembly says: "When doctrines diverge, doubt may arise; now that the multitude of sages share the same model, our doubts are extinguished.
As the Sūtra states: "As it is now with the World-Honored One, he also speaks by means of skillful expedients."
The commentary states:
This interpretation is identical to that of the Buddha’s teaching, and thus doubt is severed.
"From birth and through renunciation" refers to the skillful means of the body.
"Attaining the Way" refers to the skillful means of mind;
"turning the wheel of Dharma" refers to the skillful means of speech.
Since the initial teaching of the Three Vehicles accords with the Buddha's teachings throughout the three periods of time, it is said that he also expounds the Dharma through skillful means.
When the three karmas are discordant, doubt may arise; when form and mind are in accord, doubt is eliminated.
Furthermore, when the beginning and end of a teaching are inconsistent, doubt may arise; because the initial and final statements are consistent, doubt is extinguished.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra: "The World-Honored One taught the true path... [up to] 'this is the work of Māra,'" the commentary states:
By knowing that the tracks of the Buddha and those of Māra are different, doubt is severed.
The Māra’s words deviated from the truth, which is why doubt arose; the Buddha’s words accorded with the sublime, whereby the doubt was extinguished.
As the Sūtra says: "Hearing the Buddha’s gentle voice... until he abides in true wisdom."

The commentary states: The following fourteen verses are divided into two parts. The first twelve and a half verses conclude the severing of doubts and regrets; this final verse and a half expresses the joy of having attained peace and security. Now, hearing this, one rejoices as all afflictions are exhausted.

The middle section is further divided into two: the first twelve and a half verses conclude the elimination of doubt and remorse, while this one and a half verses represent the swift attainment of tranquility.

Because he compassionately receives and guides others, he utters gentle sounds; because he expounds the profound principles like the hidden rumble of thunder, his voice is deep and far-reaching; because it is as clear and penetrating as the song of the kalaviṅka bird and is supremely delightful, it is most subtle and wondrous; and because he discards all defilements such as fame and profit to expound the meaning of the One Vehicle, he is said to "proclaim and clarify the pure Dharma."
"Chang" (暢) means "far-reaching" and "clarifying.

Since the mind is already filled with great joy, doubt and regret are forever eliminated; one abandons the former mind that dwelt in the provisional and adopts the present wisdom that abides in the real.
The "real" refers to the One Vehicle, which is what is now sought and realized;
the "provisional" refers to the Two Vehicles, which were former expedient means.
This is as stated in the Sūtra: "I shall certainly become a Buddha... until I have taught and transformed all bodhisattvas."
The commentary states:
This verse concerns the fourth [point], knowing that the sons of the Buddha have accomplished the Way.

Now, as I am a son of the Buddha, I shall act as a Bodhisattva; born from the Mahāyāna teachings of the Buddha, having cultivated the great cause, I shall certainly become a Buddha. Outwardly revered by devas and humans, I am able to turn the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma; ultimately, I teach only the One Vehicle, and thus I am able to instruct and transform Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “At that time the Buddha addressed Śāriputra” to “...following me to receive instruction,” the commentary states:

This is the third section within the first wheel [of teaching], wherein the Tathāgata provides a formal endorsement (*anujñāna*). It is so called because it reiterates the formal endorsement in the same manner as the “Parable of the Medicinal Herbs.”
This section is divided into three parts:
first, an account of the previous encounter; second, a description of the present meeting; and third, a clarification that one must again rely on the former to grasp the reality.
This is the first part.
Regarding the statement, "Under twenty-two trillion Buddhas, he has constantly taught you for the sake of the unsurpassed path," the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* says:
"Śāriputra practiced the bodhisattva path for sixty kalpas; once, a brāhmaṇa begged him for his eyes, and Śāriputra gave them to him."
Having obtained the eye [of Dharma], he cast it upon the ground, trampled it with both feet, and departed with insults.
Śāriputra, filled with regret and remorse, subsequently withdrew from his great resolve.

This was said because at that time [the Buddha] instructed you; for twenty thousand Buddhas, he served as your spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and constantly transformed you toward the Mahāyāna, and at that time, Śāriputra likewise followed and received the teaching.
The Sūtra says: "By means of my skillful expedients, I have come to be born within my own Dharma.
The Commentary states:
This describes the present encounter.

After they have retreated from the great resolve (*mahācitta*), the Buddha, knowing that their minds fear the Great [Vehicle] and are confined to the small fruit, transforms them as Śrāvakas and causes them to realize the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). This gradual guidance and enticement is termed "expedient means" (*upāya*).

Having realized the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and given rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), they abide within the Buddha-dharma; this is called "being within my Dharma. Because they are born from the Buddha-dharma, they are truly born.

For example, Śāriputra’s lineage was regressive: his noble lineage was "near in arising but distant in ripening," which is why he initially resolved upon the Great Mind but later regressed; whereas [the lineage of] the low-born was "near in ripening but distant in arising," which is why they resolve upon the Small Mind midway and realize the fruit.
The initial teaching arises from the Great Intention (*mahāyāna*) as the cause for realizing the Truth;
the intermediate seeking of the Small [Vehicle] results in the fruition as the gradual means for relinquishing the provisional.
As the Sūtra states: "Śāriputra, having arrived, has already attained *nirvāṇa*."
The commentary states:
The following section clarifies that one must again rely on the previous [teaching] to grasp the reality; it is divided into two parts.
First, it discusses the original intent of establishing reality, which was intended for the practice of the provisional while causing one to forget the real.
Later, he manifested [the truth] to cause them to remember their original mind; by preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they returned to their original state.
This is the first [point].
"In the past, I taught you to set your will upon the Buddha-way" refers to the initial arousal of the intention for reality.

Regarding the statement, “You have now forgotten everything and yet claim for yourself that you have attained extinction (nirvāṇa),” this means that while practicing through skillful means (*upāya*), one has forgotten the reality (*tattva*).

Prior to realizing the fruit of a śrāvaka, one has not yet attained the untainted knowledge of past lives (*anāsrava-pūrvanivāsajñāna*); even if one refines one’s faculties (*indriya-pariśodhana*) for sixty kalpas and attains the śrāvaka’s untainted state, the scope of what is known by the knowledge of past lives remains relatively limited.
You have entirely forgotten the Mahāyāna you practiced in the past, and thus you claim that what you have attained is true *nirvāṇa*, refusing to advance further in your cultivation.

Regarding your statement in the previous fascicle’s request that you have already received transformation from the Buddha in life after life, yet now say you have forgotten it, there are four interpretations:
first, you yourself remember having practiced the *Hīnayāna* under the Buddha, but you have completely forgotten the Great Dharma he taught.
Second, the Buddha taught the initial Mahāyāna teachings, which [Śāriputra] has now forgotten; he remembers only that he later studied the Hīnayāna under transformation.
Third, while Śāriputra himself remembers this, others do not; because he now speaks of it by entrusting it to others, he says he has "completely forgotten" it.
Regarding the four points: previously it was said that [the Buddha] remembered because of the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); now it is said that he forgot because of his own mind.
These are not contradictory.
As the Sūtra says: "I now wish to return to the place where the Buddha dwells, to receive his protective mindfulness (*anuparigraha*)."
The commentary states:
To cause [beings] to remember their original mind, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was preached so that they might return to their source.

Initially, those of small capacity were transformed and directed toward the Great Vehicle; though termed "śrāvakas," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—the *Wonderful Dharma Lotus Sūtra*—was preached to them. Once they had turned their minds [toward enlightenment], it became known as the teaching for bodhisattvas and that which is protected by the Buddhas. Thus, one should know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* also possesses ancillary names such as the *Anantārtha*.

The essence and its function differ, and the manifestation of principle according to the capacity of the recipient varies; it is for this reason that they are divided into two sutras, as explained in the first fascicle.
The Sutra says: "Śāriputra went to the path where he was to travel."
The commentary states:
Within the fourth section of the first cycle, the Buddha bestows predictions (vyākaraṇa). This has two parts:
first, the bestowing of the prediction; second, the offerings, praises, and dedication of merit by humans and devas.
The first section is further divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the bestowal of the prophecy; second, a single verse that concludes by identifying [the present with the past] to inspire joy.
The first part contains two sections:
First, the prediction concerning the cause; second, the prediction concerning the fruit.
This first section has four parts: first, the passage of immeasurable kalpas;
second, meeting excellent conditions externally by encountering various Buddhas; third, upholding the True Dharma; and fourth, fully practicing for the benefit of sentient beings.

Because the fruit is only accomplished once the causal practices are fulfilled, it takes twenty thousand kalpas even before one enters the stage of the ten faiths; how much more so after the arousal of the mind? Thus, this first section first explains the many kalpas for the purpose of encountering various Buddhas and attaining entry into the Great Kalpa to uphold the True Dharma.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, “He shall attain Buddhahood... up to ‘Buddha, World-Honored One’,” the commentary states:
The following clarifies the prediction of the fruit (phala-vyākaraṇa), which is twofold:
First is the prose exposition, followed by the verse summary.
The prose exposition consists of six parts: first, the perfection of internal virtues;

second, the adornment of the external land; third, the teaching being identical to that of the present; fourth, the name of the kalpa being different from that of the present; fifth, the superiority or inferiority of the attendant bodhisattvas; and sixth, the brevity or length of the duration of the Dharma.
This is the first [meaning].

His eyes behold the rain of flowers and the emission of light; his ears hear the Dharma-flower and the light of wisdom. Furthermore, externally he partakes of the secret Dharma, while internally the light of wisdom arises. Because of these two meanings, he is named Huaguang (Flower-Light).

Now, the principles for recording the names of Buddhas are not uniform. For instance, Śākyamuni and Maitreya were named based on their observation of those respective Buddhas; likewise, Śāriputra initially had his title established based on what he had seen and heard.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Three hundred bhikṣus removed their robes and offered them to the Buddha, who raised his hand as a gesture; they were prophesied to become the Tathāgata Mahālakṣaṇa.
Furthermore, a thousand devaputras, seeing the adornment of the Buddha-field, gave rise to pure intentions; they were prophesied to become the Buddha Vyūharāja."

Furthermore, in that "Chapter on the Tongue-Phenomenon" (*jihvā-viśeṣa-parivarta*), it says: "One hundred trillion people saw the Bodhisattvas from the ten directions coming and making offerings with flowers; they gave rise to the resolve for awakening and received their predictions. The Buddha's name shall be Awakening Flower (*Bodhi-puṣpa*), and the eon shall be named Accumulation of Flowers (*Puṣpa-rāśi*)."

Such categories as these cannot be standardized; in some cases, these may all be Buddhas encountered at the very beginning, and later meeting with these conditions serves as a cause that accords with past vows.
The bestowal of predictions (vyākaraṇa) is briefly analyzed by way of six sections: first, the causes for the bestowal of prediction;

second, who is able to bestow the prediction; third, whom the prediction is bestowed upon; fourth, the distinctions among predictions; fifth, the resolution of objections; and sixth, the differences among the classes of śrāvakas.
The reasons for bestowing the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) are briefly summarized by five points:

First, as the treatise states, it is for the purpose of generating a resolute mind in the śrāvakas; it is not because they have perfected the *dharmatā*. They are not predicted based on having already realized the *dharmatā* of the two kinds of emptiness, but rather the prediction is given so that they may develop the resolve to advance toward the Mahāyāna.

The two treatises state that because the nature of the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* is equal, the three vehicles are taught due to the differences among conditioned phenomena; yet since the ultimate truth is identical, there is no difference in the *dharmakāya*.

Third, it is to eliminate the long-standing doubts of bodhisattvas; for they had long doubted that śrāvakas could become buddhas, but now, upon hearing their prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), those long-standing doubts are extinguished.
Fourth, it is so that those who rejoice in the Buddha, upon seeing this prediction, may rejoice in the thought that they themselves shall likewise attain the practice of the causes of buddhahood.
The reason for explaining the ten meanings of the One Vehicle in five ways is precisely the basis for the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) herein.
Within that which can bestow predictions, there are three parts:
first, the basis; second, the essence of the prediction; and third, the function of the prediction.
Regarding the basis that is capable of bestowing prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), six aspects are manifested: five are predictions of the Tathāgata, and one is a prediction of a bodhisattva.
As for the predictions of the Tathāgata:
first, individual prediction; second, collective prediction; third, subsequent prediction; fourth, prediction without enmity; and fifth, prediction of universal practice.

The prediction (vyākaraṇa) of a bodhisattva is called the "prediction based on possessing the cause. As demonstrated in the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging" (*Sadāparibhūta-parivarta*), [the Buddha] manifested prostration and praise, saying, "I do not slight you; you shall all become buddhas," because he showed that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). He grants this prediction of their future buddha-name; only a Buddha can grant such a prediction, as other sages cannot, for they are unable to specifically know the names of future buddhas, their lands, and so forth—those of lower status cannot know the affairs of those above them.
However, if the prediction is made in a manner that is implicit or contained within the teaching, a bodhisattva may also receive it, because they likewise possess the cause of buddha-nature.
Since this sūtra is thus, among all sūtras, the conferring of predictions does not exceed these two types.
The essence of the prediction refers to the subsequently attained conventional wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

The function of the prediction refers to verbal instruction; it takes as its essence whichever of the five aggregates is appropriate for the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) or Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), because there are differences between the ten stages of bodhisattvas and the three vehicles.
There are two aspects to the bestowal of a prediction:
first, the basis; second, the essential nature.
The basis refers to the one who is the recipient of the prediction.
The Treatise states:
"There are six types of manifestations:

first, individual prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). Because the names and titles of the four great śrāvakas—Śāriputra, Mahākāśyapa, and others—who are well-known to the assembly, are distinct, they are given individual predictions."
Second, the simultaneous prediction (*sahābhiṣeka*), because five hundred people such as Pūrṇa and twelve hundred others share the same name, they are given their predictions at the same time.

Third, the subsequent prediction (*paścād-abhiṣeka*); although those who are still training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) share a common title and are of inferior faculties unknown to the assembly, they are nevertheless given their predictions later.
The fourth is the prediction of enmitylessness, given to Devadatta, which demonstrates that the Tathāgata is free from resentment and malice.

The fifth is the prediction of universal practice, given to the bhikṣuṇīs and the goddesses, which demonstrates that women—whether lay or ordained—who cultivate the bodhisattva path shall all realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
"The prediction based on the six causes (*ṣaḍ-hetu-vyākaraṇa*) demonstrates that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature.

These six types of predictions are recorded individually in the "Parable Chapter" (*Upamā-parivarta*) and the "Bestowal of Predictions Chapter" (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*); they are recorded collectively in the "Chapter on the Prediction for the Five Hundred Disciples" (*Pañcaśata-śrāvaka-vyākaraṇa-parivarta*); the prediction for those without resentment is recorded in the "Devadatta Chapter" (*Devadatta-parivarta*); the prediction for universal practice is recorded in the "Dharma Master Chapter" (*Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*) and the "Upholding Chapter" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*); and the prediction based on the six causes is recorded in the "Chapter on Never Disparaging" (*Sadāparibhūta-parivarta*).

Inferring by means of reason, those who receive the prediction are these four types of persons: ordinary beings who have not yet generated the aspiration for enlightenment, those who have already generated it, those of the two vehicles with indeterminate nature, and all bodhisattvas.

The single assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is for the purpose of transforming [beings] so that they relinquish the provisional and attain the real; therefore, it bestows predictions of enlightenment upon bodhisattvas of the ten stages who have attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

When discussing ancient events, there are predictions regarding those who possessed the causes prior to generating the aspiration for awakening; however, for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who generate the aspiration thereafter, there is no one who hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and does not become a Buddha. This constitutes the prediction for those of the two vehicles whose lineage is indeterminate, and there is nothing else besides this.
The essence of the cause is the untainted wholesome root (*anāsrava-kuśalamūla*), encompassing both the manifest and the seeds.

The essence of the fruit obtained through that cause comprises all five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). These are predominantly *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation bodies) and *saṃbhogakāya* for others, because they manifest compassion, manifest the loftiness of virtue, possess distinctions, and transform sentient beings; these points shall be fully demonstrated in the subsequent predictions (*vyākaraṇa*).

Regarding the distinctions among the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* states: "The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Resolute Mind (Dṛḍhamati): 'There are four kinds of predictions bestowed: there is the prediction bestowed before one has yet resolved for enlightenment;

there is the prediction bestowed at the very moment one resolves for enlightenment; there is the secret prediction; and there is the prediction bestowed in the presence of others upon attaining the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). These are called the four kinds.'"
"Only the Tathāgata can know this matter.
The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* also speaks in the same way.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter forty-six, states that, briefly, there are six characteristics by which one receives the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) from all Tathāgatas regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
What are the six?

First, the stage of abiding in the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) before having generated the resolve for enlightenment; second, the stage of having already generated that resolve; third, the stage of being present before one's eyes; and fourth, the stage of not being present before one's eyes.

These four aforementioned types are the same as those in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*. Regarding "secret prediction" (*guhya-vyākaraṇa*), it refers to that which is not manifest because it occurs in a secret place;

alternatively, for those who have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), it is called "manifest," while for those who have not yet attained it, it is called "non-manifest.

Alternatively, when one's body is present in the assembly, it is called "manifest," and when the body is not in the assembly, it is called "non-manifest. This is confirmed by the fourth fascicle below, where among those with identical predictions, there are some not present in the assembly, and the Buddha commands that their prediction be transmitted to them.
Fifth, there is a fixed time limit, meaning that one shall realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment within such a period.
Sixth, there is no fixed time limit, meaning that one is granted a prophecy without specifying a definitive time frame.

Now, Śāriputra corresponds to the second, third, and sixth stages; because he has already resolved upon the Great Mind (mahācitta), dwells before the Buddha, and there is no fixed time limit. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"The Srotāpanna arrives after eighty thousand kalpas, up to the Arhat who arrives after twenty thousand kalpas, and the Pratyekabuddha who arrives after ten thousand kalpas. What is meant by "arriving" is arriving at the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; thus we know that after such kalpas have passed, one finally reaches the initial mind of the Ten Faiths and begins to enter the first kalpa.

The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "Circuitous practice is not as [effective] as that of a bodhisattva who has newly begun their initial career, because the latter’s attachment to the flavor of quiescence is extremely profound."
Therefore, the present statement that one must pass through immeasurable kalpas before finally making offerings to several tens of billions of buddhas and practicing the bodhisattva path,
and so forth, involves three certainties:
first, the certainty of lineage, whereby upon encountering the necessary conditions, one is able to realize perfect enlightenment.
Second is the certainty of generating the resolve: having generated the great resolve, one never again regresses;
third is non-empty conduct: having attained mastery, one never allows the benefit of sentient beings to go to waste.
First, it is before the stages, because among the five kinds of bodhi, it is the bodhi of generating the mind;
next, it is in the first stage, because it is the bodhi of realizing the generation of the mind;
and finally, it is in the eighth stage.
Now, based on the first dhyāna, they are granted the prediction (vyākaraṇa).

To resolve this objection, the treatise asks: "Is it that these śrāvakas and others are predicted because they will truly attain Buddhahood, or is it that they are granted the prediction despite not attaining Buddhahood?"
If he has truly attained Buddhahood, for what reason would the Bodhisattva have cultivated and accumulated immeasurable merit over immeasurable kalpas?
If he has not attained Buddhahood, how could he have bestowed a prediction of enlightenment that is false?
This intention is difficult to express.

If śrāvakas and others, by merely abiding for a hundred kalpas or more while refining their faculties and practicing the śrāvaka path, were to truly attain Buddhahood and receive a prediction [of enlightenment], then for what reason would bodhisattvas need to cultivate and accumulate immeasurable merit over immeasurable kalpas before attaining the bodhi of a Buddha? For they would have already been able to truly become Buddhas through those minor causes.
If śrāvakas and others cannot achieve [Buddhahood] despite cultivating minor causes, why would there be a need for this present false prediction?

The treatise itself answers: "The prediction granted to those śrāvakas is for the sake of attaining a mind of certainty, not because they have accomplished the *dharmatā*. This means that it is intended to cause the śrāvakas and others to attain a mind certain of achieving Buddhahood so that they may advance in the cultivation of sublime practices; it does not mean that they have already realized and attained the truth of the *dharmatā* of the two kinds of emptiness and are therefore granted the prediction.

The treatise further explains: "The Tathāgata, relying on the equality of the three vehicles, teaches the Dharma of the One Vehicle; he bestows predictions because the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is no different from the Dharma-body of those śrāvakas, not because they have already fully perfected the cultivation of meritorious virtues."

Because Bodhisattvas of the ten stages have accomplished the Dharma, they are fully endowed with merit; whereas the Śrāvakas are not yet fully endowed with merit. For this reason, a Bodhisattva must cultivate immeasurable practices before attaining Bodhi, while a Śrāvaka has not yet cultivated immeasurable merit, but because he has caused the mind for Buddhahood to become settled, he is granted a prediction [of enlightenment].”
Question:
Since the Śrāvaka who has attained the state beyond training (aśaikṣa) has forever exhausted future existence, why is it recorded in the sūtras that he shall attain bodhi after three great kalpas?
Answer:
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that [the body] "is based on the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), not a body produced as the fruit of karma";

thus, it does not contradict reason. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that "this is another name for the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmikī cyuti*). This means that prior to generating the resolve for enlightenment, the manifested body is limited; however, after receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) and generating the great vow to seek great awakening (*mahābodhi*) and deliver sentient beings, one enters the supreme untainted meditative absorption of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-anāsrava-samādhi*). This sustains the karma performed in the past that brought about the present body, causing it to continue yielding its fruit over a long period without interruption.

The karma that serves as the sustenance for this [transformation] is nourished by the untainted (*anāsrava*); through this gradual refinement, the former coarse maturation (*vipāka*) becomes subsequently subtle, vast, and exceptionally wondrous, differing from its original state. Because it is like a magical creation (*nirmāṇa*), and because it differs from the previous state through this transformation, it is called "transformation-death" (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*). It is sustained and increased repeatedly until the attainment of Buddhahood. Although the *prātibhāsa-cyuti* (segmented death) has been forever exhausted, it is said that after passing three hundred *yojana*, one creates a city; yet because the *pariṇāmi-cyuti* is not yet exhausted, it is said that one must travel another two hundred *yojana* before reaching the Precious Place (*ratnasthāna*).

Although the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*prātibhāgika-jarāmaraṇa*) is forever exhausted for all, those Śrāvakas who seek quiescence lack the capacity to undergo transformational birth (*pariṇāmi-jāti*) until they attain Buddhahood;

therefore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "With the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) as the condition and untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) as the cause, there arise the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) of Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of great power."
This is explained in detail in separate chapters of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, among others.
Regarding the differences among the śrāvaka types, the treatise states that there are four:
first, those who are determined; second, those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*); third, those who have regressed from the bodhicitta; and fourth, those who are emanations (*nirmāṇa*).

The Tathāgata grants two kinds of predictions: namely, for those who are emanations and for those who have regressed from the bodhicitta. With the exception of those who are fixed in their destiny and those with overweening pride—because their faculties are not yet mature—the Tathāgata does not grant them a prediction.

The Bodhisattva bestows a prediction (vyākaraṇa); because the Bodhisattva bestows a prediction as a skillful means to inspire the arousal of the mind of enlightenment, this refers to the prediction of "Never-Disparaging.
One might say that those who are immature or those with overweening pride (adhimāna) can be described thus;
however, regarding those who have entered ultimate quiescence (śamaikāyana), they are never mature—how then can one say they are merely "immature"?

"Un-" means "not. According to the underlying principle, it should be stated that those who have entered quiescence are not deluded regarding the Dharma; however, because their faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is not yet mature, the Buddha does not grant them a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). This is because he does not clearly predict that they will become Buddhas in a future life.

As for the Bodhisattvas granting predictions, there is a logical basis for this as they contain the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*); thus, through skillful means (*upāya*), they cause [those beings] to give rise to the mind of faith in the Mahāyāna.
For those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), whose faculties of faith and inclination are not yet mature, the Buddha does not clearly predict their future attainment of Buddhahood;
nor does the Bodhisattva grant them a prediction, employing skillful means instead to cause them to develop a mind of faith and inclination.
Now, combining these points, the text states that because their faculties are not yet mature, those who do not seek quiescence shall also be able to attain Buddhahood.
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* says: "The roots of virtue of other persons are exhausted at the time of nirvāṇa, but the roots of virtue of Bodhisattvas are not so."

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that "to say that those such as the *srotāpanna* will all attain Buddhahood is to fail to understand my intention. Therefore, we know that those who have entered the concentration of ultimate quiescence do not become Buddhas.

Regarding those who are śrāvakas through transformation, some say they consist of the four great śrāvakas of superior faculties such as Śāriputra, the five hundred of middling faculties, and those in training and those beyond training of inferior faculties.

Now, this interpretation is not correct. In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is stated at the beginning that Śāriputra is an emanation; however, later, when he enters the "Dharmadhātu Chapter," Śāriputra leads six thousand disciples out from his own chamber, and Mañjuśrī expounds the ten dharmas for him, whereupon he resolves upon bodhicitta. Since he receives a prediction of enlightenment within this very context, he is not merely an emanation.

Śāriputra alone was a śrāvaka of superior capacity; the four great disciples were of middling capacity, and the five hundred others were of inferior capacity. According to the subsequent sutra, it is stated that Pūrṇa and the others were those who appeared as transformations for this single assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

As explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* within the section on the ten meanings of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), this accords with the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and other scriptures: śrāvakas who have entered nirvāṇa after many kalpas become intoxicated and lie prostrate by drinking the wine of samādhi; later, they arise from that concentration and resolve their minds toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). These are all emanations (*nirmāṇa*) created by the Buddhas and bodhisattvas for the purpose of guiding other classes of beings.
